name: Hacking pockets / slanted pockets

lead:
Hacking pockets are jacket pockets set at an angle instead of horizontally. They belong to the hacking jacket, a tweed sports coat historically made for casual horseback riding.
Style writers describe the slant as drawing the eye diagonally and giving the torso a more tapered, dressier line, so a jacket with them is often chosen for a slimmer-looking waist.

paras: People choose a jacket or blazer cut with slanted flap pockets, often with a single vent and a fitted waist. Tailors can also specify them on bespoke or made-to-measure jackets. They are usually worn closed or lightly used so the line is kept clean.
There is no health risk. Overfilled pockets of any kind change the way a jacket hangs.

chain: Looks like a slimmer, more tapered torso
angle.text: The slant is said to break up the width of the jacket at the hip and lead the eye toward the waist. Wearers use it as a style detail alongside a good fit.

lead: Hacking pockets, also called slanted pockets, are jacket pockets cut at an angle rather than horizontally. They are associated with the hacking jacket, a wool sports coat for casual horseback riding, often in tweed.[1]

People use them as a tailoring choice to change the line of a jacket. Style commentary commonly says the slant creates a longer, slimmer-looking waist and a more dynamic silhouette, and that the angle suits shorter frames. This is a matter of style opinion and no published study has tested the effect.

The Wikipedia article on the hacking jacket describes the garment as traditionally three-buttoned with a single vent, a statement it marks as needing a citation, and says sports coats first appeared for outdoor country sports such as shooting and riding.[1]

paras: The hacking jacket is a wool sports coat intended for casual riding, often in tweed, and traditionally three-buttoned with a single vent.[1] Slanted pockets are the angled flap pockets characteristic of the style; Wikipedia's article notes that sports coats generally have flap pockets, unlike blazers that often have patch pockets.[1]

Sports coats were first worn for outdoor country sports such as shooting and riding before spreading to spectators and everyday wear.[1] Commonly given explanations for the angle relate to reaching the pockets from the saddle, though this is repeated in style writing rather than established.
In style-focused discussions the slant is cited as a way to make the waist look slimmer. These are style opinions rather than measured effects.
